summary: Liechtenstein applies Schengen rules through its association agreement: EU/EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period, and everyone else needs a Schengen visa — issued on Liechtenstein's behalf by Swiss missions, since the principality has no airport and is entered via Switzerland or Austria.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Applications are handled by Swiss embassies and visa centres on Liechtenstein's behalf; a visa valid for Switzerland covers Liechtenstein.

source.name: Liechtenstein National Administration — Migration and Passport Office

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

source.name: Liechtenstein National Administration — Migration and Passport Office

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

source.name: Liechtenstein National Administration — Migration and Passport Office

proofOfFunds.text: Swiss border authorities, who control entry to Liechtenstein, use a guideline of around CHF 100 per person per day (about CHF 30 for students) — sufficiency is assessed case by case. Confirm current expectations with the Swiss mission handling your visa.

source.name: Liechtenstein National Administration — Migration and Passport Office

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Liechtenstein has no external Schengen border of its own — biometric EES registration (fingerprints and photo) happens when you first enter the Schengen Area, for example at a Swiss or Austrian airport. Allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorisation System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Liechtenstein forms a customs union with Switzerland, so Swiss customs rules apply: cash of CHF 10,000 or more must be declared if customs officers ask.

source.name: Liechtenstein National Administration — Migration and Passport Office

notes: Goods allowances follow Swiss rules, not EU rules — duty-free limits apply even when arriving from EU countries such as Austria.
There are no systematic border checks when entering from Switzerland; spot customs checks are possible on the Austrian border.

payments.text: Cards and contactless are accepted nearly everywhere. Both Swiss francs and euros are taken in most shops, though prices are set in francs and change is given in francs at unfavourable rates.

safety.text: Liechtenstein is one of the safest countries in the world, with negligible crime. The only practical hazards are alpine ones — check conditions before mountain hikes.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Liechtenstein Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Late spring to early autumn is best for hiking the Rhine valley and the alpine trails above Vaduz; December brings a small Christmas market and the start of the ski season in Malbun.

tips.text: Liechtenstein has no airport — fly to Zurich (about 115 km away), take a train to Sargans or Buchs and continue by Liechtenstein Bus to Vaduz. There are no systematic passport checks when crossing from Switzerland or Austria.
Liechtenstein issues no visas of its own — Schengen visa applications are handled by Swiss embassies, and a visa valid for Switzerland also covers Liechtenstein.
The Swiss franc is the currency. Euros are widely accepted in shops and restaurants, but you get change in francs at a rounded, unfavourable rate — pay by card instead.
There is no border stamp on arrival — the Vaduz tourist office sells a souvenir Liechtenstein passport stamp for a few francs if you want proof of your visit.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Liechtenstein?
faq.answer: Liechtenstein follows Schengen rules: EU/EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely, and visa-exempt nationalities (US, UK, Canada, Japan and about 60 others) can stay 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa — any valid Schengen visa covers Liechtenstein.

faq.question: How do I get to Liechtenstein without an airport?
faq.answer: Fly to Zurich (or Munich/Innsbruck), take a train to Sargans or Buchs in Switzerland, or Feldkirch in Austria, then a Liechtenstein Bus to Vaduz — about 1.5–2 hours from Zurich in total. There are no systematic border checks on entry from either country.

faq.question: Does Liechtenstein issue its own visas?
faq.answer: No. Under its Schengen association, Switzerland represents Liechtenstein for visa matters — you apply at the Swiss embassy or visa centre serving your place of residence, and a visa valid for Switzerland is valid for Liechtenstein.

faq.question: Does time in Liechtenstein count toward my 90 Schengen days?
faq.answer: Yes. Liechtenstein is part of the Schengen Area, so days spent there count toward the same 90-days-in-180 limit as the rest of the area.

faq.question: What currency does Liechtenstein use?
faq.answer: The Swiss franc (CHF). Euros are accepted in most shops at a rounded exchange rate with change in francs, so cards or francs are the better way to pay.
